title: Literary Analysis — Craft and Structure
description: Analyze how authors develop plot, character, and theme through craft choices.
objectives: Analyze plot structure with precision
Explain how an author's word choices shape meaning
Evaluate how multiple themes interact

lessons.title: Analyzing Author's Craft
lessons.content: Every word choice, structural decision, and narrative technique is intentional.
examples: Foreshadowing: early hints that create suspense ('Little did she know that...')
Flashback: moves back in time to reveal background
Unreliable narrator: the narrator's perspective is limited or distorted

lessons.title: Multiple Themes
lessons.content: Complex literary works often have several interrelated themes.
examples: The Outsiders: themes of class conflict, loyalty, and identity all intersect
One event can develop multiple themes simultaneously

title: Argumentative Writing
description: Plan and write a formal argumentative essay with claim, evidence, and counterargument.
objectives: Write a debatable thesis/claim
Use relevant evidence from credible sources
Effectively address counterarguments

lessons.title: Thesis and Structure
lessons.content: A strong thesis is specific, debatable, and previews main reasons.
examples: Weak: 'Homework has pros and cons'
Strong: 'Nightly homework should be eliminated for middle schoolers because it increases stress, reduces family time, and fails to improve academic achievement'

lessons.title: Counterargument and Rebuttal
lessons.content: Acknowledge opposing views, then refute them with evidence.
examples: 'Some argue that homework builds responsibility; however, research indicates that self-directed reading is more effective for developing independent learners'

title: Reading Nonfiction — Rhetorical Analysis
description: Analyze the rhetorical strategies authors use to persuade in nonfiction texts.
objectives: Identify ethos, pathos, and logos
Analyze how word choice and structure support the argument
Evaluate the effectiveness of persuasion

lessons.title: Rhetorical Appeals
lessons.content: Persuasive writers appeal to credibility, emotion, and logic.
examples: Ethos: 'As a doctor with 20 years of experience...' (credibility)
Pathos: a story about a child suffering from pollution (emotion)
Logos: statistics showing 80% of scientists agree on climate change (logic)

lessons.title: Analyzing Language
lessons.content: Word choice (diction) and tone shape how readers feel about the argument.
examples: 'Militants' vs. 'freedom fighters' — same people, very different connotation
Formal, objective language builds credibility; passionate language builds emotion

title: Grammar — Phrases and Clauses
description: Identify and correctly use phrases and clauses to add variety and precision.
objectives: Identify noun, verb, adjective, and adverb phrases
Use participial and infinitive phrases
Write sentences with varied clause structures

lessons.title: Phrases
lessons.content: A phrase lacks a subject-verb pair and cannot stand alone.
examples: Prepositional phrase: 'under the old bridge'
Participial phrase: 'Running through the rain, she finally reached home'
Infinitive phrase: 'To win the championship was her goal'

lessons.title: Varied Sentence Structure
examples: Simple: 'She ran.'
Compound: 'She ran, but she was too late.'
Complex: 'Although she ran as fast as she could, she missed the train.'

title: Research — Synthesis Writing
description: Synthesize information from multiple sources into a coherent research essay.
objectives: Integrate evidence from 4+ sources
Write without plagiarism; cite correctly
Synthesize rather than simply summarize sources

lessons.title: Synthesis vs. Summary
lessons.content: Synthesis weaves ideas from multiple sources together around YOUR argument.
examples: Summary: 'Source A says X. Source B says Y.'
Synthesis: 'Multiple experts agree that X (Source A; Source B), while Source C offers the counterpoint that Y'

title: Reading Across Genres — Comparing Texts
description: Compare how different genres handle the same topic or theme.
objectives: Compare a poem, story, and nonfiction text on the same theme
Analyze what each genre can and cannot do
Evaluate which treatment is most effective

lessons.title: Genre Comparison
lessons.content: The same subject can be explored through different lenses.
examples: Topic: war. Compare: a war poem (Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est'), a novel excerpt (All Quiet on the Western Front), a news article
Each form uses different techniques to create impact

title: Vocabulary — Academic Language
description: Build academic vocabulary for reading, writing, and discussion across subjects.
objectives: Identify Tier 2 academic vocabulary
Use context and morphology to infer meaning
Apply academic vocabulary in writing

lessons.title: Tier 2 Vocabulary
lessons.content: Academic words appear across subjects and in formal writing.
examples: Analyze, evaluate, synthesize, justify, interpret, infer
These words appear on standardized tests and in college writing
Learn them in context rather than memorizing definitions

title: Drama — Reading and Performance
description: Read, analyze, and perform dramatic texts.
objectives: Analyze dialogue and stage directions
Compare a dramatic text to its film adaptation
Perform a scene with attention to character and tone

lessons.title: Reading Drama
lessons.content: Drama is meant to be performed; read with performance in mind.
examples: Stage directions give clues about setting, mood, and character
Subtext: what characters mean beyond what they literally say
Cast plays strategically when reading aloud in class

lessons.title: Adaptation Analysis
lessons.content: Compare a play to its film adaptation — what changes and why?
examples: Some dialogue is cut in films; scenes may be added
Consider: what can film do that a stage cannot? What can a stage do that film cannot?

title: Personal Narrative
description: Write a personal narrative that conveys a meaningful experience with reflection.
objectives: Choose a meaningful event
Use literary techniques in personal writing
Reflect on significance — not just what happened but why it mattered

lessons.title: Crafting the Narrative
lessons.content: Great personal narratives use literary techniques to create meaning.
examples: Start in the middle of action (in medias res)
Use sensory details: sight, sound, smell, taste, touch
'I remember the exact smell of rain on hot pavement that afternoon...'

lessons.title: Reflection
lessons.content: The reflection is the most important part — it shows what you learned or how you changed.
examples: Move beyond description to meaning: 'That moment taught me...'
Connect the personal to the universal: how does your experience relate to larger human experiences?

title: Independent Reading and Book Clubs
description: Develop as independent readers through choice reading and collaborative discussion.
objectives: Read independently for sustained periods
Discuss books in a small-group book club format
Write reader's response and book review

lessons.title: Reader's Response
lessons.content: Respond personally and analytically to what you read.
examples: Personal: 'This character reminded me of...because...'
Analytical: 'The author uses foreshadowing in chapter 3 when...'
Evaluative: 'I think the ending was unsatisfying because...'

lessons.title: Book Club Discussion
lessons.content: Book clubs thrive on genuine questions and diverse perspectives.
examples: Ask genuine questions you don't know the answer to
'I was confused by... Can anyone explain...?'
'What I found most interesting was... Does anyone disagree?'
